title: News feed (Twitter/X home timeline)
tagline: Show each user a fresh, ranked feed from the accounts they follow, in under 200 ms, while celebrities post to 50M followers.
summary: Two numbers shape this design: reads outnumber posts by tens of times, and each post must reach every follower. So you precompute. When someone posts, workers push the new tweet ID into each follower's cached timeline (fan-out on write), and reading a feed becomes one Redis call plus a hydrate. Celebrities break that model (one post would mean 50M cache writes), so their tweets are pulled at read time and merged in. That mix is the hybrid model, and it is the answer interviewers are looking for.

functional: Post a tweet: up to 280 characters plus photos or video
Home timeline: tweets from accounts you follow, ranked or newest first, paginated
Profile timeline: one user's own tweets
nonfunctional: Home timeline p99 under ~200 ms; it is the first screen of the app
A new tweet reaches followers' feeds within a few seconds (eventual consistency is fine)
Highly available for reads: a stale feed beats an error page
Handle accounts with tens of millions of followers without slowing everyone else
out_of_scope: Ads and the details of the ranking model

api.desc: Returns {media_id, upload_url}. The client PUTs the file straight to object storage.
Returns 201 {tweet_id}. Fan-out happens after the response.
Returns {tweets[], next_cursor}. The cursor is the last tweet ID seen, not a page number.
Profile timeline, read straight from the author index.
Follow. DELETE the same path to unfollow.

data.name: tweets
data.note: Shard by hash of tweet_id so writes spread evenly. A second index on (author_id, tweet_id DESC) serves profiles and celebrity pulls.

data.name: follows
data.note: Stored twice: keyed by follower (who do I follow?) and by followee (who follows me?), each sharded on its first column.

data.name: users
data.note: Fan-out workers read is_celebrity and last_active_at to decide who gets a push.

data.name: timeline:{user_id}
data.note: A cache, not the source of truth. Any timeline can be rebuilt from follows + tweets.

flows.name: Post (normal user)
flows.desc: Fan-out on write: about 200 cache writes per tweet.

steps.note: Any photo goes first, straight to object storage with a presigned URL from POST /v1/media. A 3 MB image never passes through your app servers; the tweet carries only media_id.
POST /v1/tweets {text, media_ids}. The gateway checks the session token and a per-user rate limit, because spam bots post thousands of times a minute.
Routed to any post-service replica. It is stateless, so you add replicas for load.
Write the tweet with a Snowflake ID: 64 bits of timestamp + machine + sequence, so sorting by ID is sorting by time. This row is the source of truth; everything after it can be rebuilt.
Publish TweetCreated{id, author} to Kafka. Partition by author so one author's tweets stay in order.
Return 201 in about 50 ms. The poster does not wait for 200 follower timelines; they update in the background over the next second or two.
A fan-out worker consumes the event. If it crashes mid-way, Kafka redelivers. Pushing the same ID twice is harmless because the reader dedupes by ID.
Read the follower list in pages of a few thousand. Skip followers inactive for 30+ days: their timeline is rebuilt on demand if they ever return, which saves most of the writes.
Per follower: LPUSH timeline:{id} tweet_id then LTRIM 0 799. Only the 8-byte ID goes in, never the text, so a tweet edit or delete changes one row, not 200 copies.

flows.name: Post (celebrity)
flows.desc: Why pure fan-out on write breaks.

steps.note: An account with 50M followers posts.
Same entry path as anyone else.
Same durable write, indexed by (author_id, tweet_id) so it can be read by author later.
Same event onto the queue.

The worker reads is_celebrity. Above a threshold (say 100k followers, tuned from data) it skips fan-out. 50M LPUSHes would take about a minute of the whole cluster's write capacity and delay every other tweet queued behind it.
The tweet simply waits in the tweet store. Followers pull it when they open the app: one extra indexed read per celebrity they follow, merged at read time.

flows.name: Read home timeline
flows.desc: One cache read, a short celebrity pull, hydrate, rank.

steps.note: GET /v1/timeline/home?limit=20. This runs tens of thousands of times a second, so every hop must be a cache or an indexed read.
Routed to the timeline service, which does the merge.
One Redis call returns up to 800 precomputed tweet IDs, about 1 ms. On a miss (a user back after months) rebuild from the graph and tweet store: slow once, then cached.
Which accounts I follow are celebrities? Usually tens, and the answer is cached per user.

Pull each celebrity's recent tweets by author index, merge with the cached IDs by Snowflake ID, then hydrate: one multi-get for the tweet bodies, served mostly from the tweet cache. Drop deleted tweets and blocked authors here.
Score the few hundred candidates (recency, likes, how often you interact with the author) and keep the top 20. A chronological 'Latest' tab skips this step.
Return 20 tweets and next_cursor (the last tweet ID). Media come back as URLs, not bytes.
The app loads images from a nearby CDN edge. Popular media hit the cache well over 90% of the time.
A miss fetches once from object storage; every later viewer nearby gets the cached copy.

deep.title: Fan-out on write, on read, or both?
deep.html:
• Fan-out on write (push): precompute every follower's feed when a tweet is posted. Reads are one cache call. Cost: write amplification (1 post × followers) and wasted work for followers who never log in.
  • Fan-out on read (pull): at read time, fetch recent tweets from every account you follow and merge. No wasted writes, but following 500 accounts means 500 lookups on every refresh, at 58k reads/s.
  • Hybrid: push for normal accounts, pull for the few accounts above a follower threshold, merge at read time. Twitter described this approach publicly in its 2013 'Timelines at Scale' talk (Redis timelines capped at 800 entries, replicated 3 times).

Say the threshold out loud and say it is tunable: the cost of a push grows with followers, the cost of a pull grows with how many readers follow that account.

deep.title: Sharding the tweet store and hot keys
deep.html: Shard tweets by a hash of tweet_id. If you range-shard by time-ordered ID, every new write lands on the newest shard. If you shard by author, a celebrity's shard becomes hot. A viral tweet is a hot read key instead: put it in an in-process cache on each timeline server for a few seconds, so 100k reads/s on one tweet never reach one cache node. Try both modes and the celebrity toggle below.

deep.title: Pagination with cursors
deep.html: Use ?cursor=<last tweet_id>, not ?page=3. New tweets arrive at the top while you scroll, so offset pages shift and show duplicates. A cursor says 'older than this ID', which is stable because Snowflake IDs are time-ordered. The 800-entry cache covers a few days of scrolling; past that, fall back to pulling from the tweet store.

deep.title: Deletes, unfollows and blocks
deep.html: Do not try to remove a deleted tweet from 50M cached lists. Mark it deleted in the tweet store and filter at hydrate time, which you already do for every read. Same for unfollow and block: filter on read now, and let an async job trim the cached list later. On a new follow, an async job backfills that account's last ~20 tweets into your timeline so the feed does not look empty.

tradeoffs.choice: Fan-out on write or on read?
tradeoffs.why: Push gives cheap reads for the 99.9% of accounts with modest followings; pull avoids 50M writes per celebrity post. The merge costs a few extra indexed reads per request.

tradeoffs.choice: What goes in the timeline cache?
tradeoffs.why: 8 B per entry keeps the cache at ~1.6 TB instead of hundreds of TB, and edits and deletes touch one row. You pay one multi-get to hydrate.

tradeoffs.pick: Ranked by default, with a 'Latest' tab
tradeoffs.why: Ranking lifts engagement but needs a scoring step and features. Keep chronological as a fallback when the ranker is slow or down.

tradeoffs.choice: How fresh must the feed be?
tradeoffs.why: Nobody notices a 2 s delay on a new tweet. Requiring it to be synchronous would put 200+ cache writes on the poster's request.

bottlenecks.issue: A big event (New Year, a final) triples posts for an hour
bottlenecks.fix: Kafka absorbs the burst, workers autoscale on consumer lag, and active users are fanned out first. Feeds lag by seconds, nothing fails.

bottlenecks.issue: A viral tweet is read 100k times a second
bottlenecks.fix: Short-lived in-process cache on each timeline server plus replicated hot keys in the tweet cache, so no single node takes all the reads.
Each list has replicas; on a total miss rebuild from the graph and tweet store. The cache is disposable by design.

followups.q: How do you show the '5 new posts' banner?
followups.a: The client polls a cheap endpoint with since_id every 30-60 s (or keeps a WebSocket open). The server compares against the head of the cached list and returns a count. It never builds the full feed for this.

followups.q: Someone follows 2,000 accounts and logs in after a year away. What happens?
followups.a: Their cached timeline was never filled (inactive users are skipped) or expired. Rebuild on demand: pull recent tweets from the accounts they follow, merge, cache, return. The first load is slower; show a spinner and cap the pull at the most recently active followees.

followups.q: Where does the threshold for 'celebrity' come from?
followups.a: Data. Push cost grows with follower count; pull cost grows with how many active readers follow that account. Start around 10k-100k followers, measure fan-out lag and read latency, then tune. It can differ per account (an active celebrity vs a dormant one).

Write each tweet in the author's home region and replicate the event stream. Each region runs its own fan-out workers and timeline caches for users who live there. A tweet from across the world shows up after replication lag, which is fine for a feed.

followups.q: How does ranking scale to 170k requests a second?
followups.a: Two stages: cheap candidate generation (the ~800 IDs plus celebrity pulls) and a light model that scores only those. Precompute author and tweet features asynchronously; keep model inference per request under ~50 ms, and fall back to chronological if it times out.

quiz.q: Why not fan out a 50M-follower account's tweet on write?
options: Redis lists can't hold that many entries
It turns one post into 50M writes and delays every tweet queued behind it
quiz.why: Write amplification. Pull those few accounts at read time and merge instead.

quiz.q: What should the timeline cache store?
options: Tweet IDs, hydrated at read time
quiz.why: IDs are 8 bytes, and edits or deletes change one row instead of millions of copies.

quiz.q: Why paginate with a cursor of the last tweet ID instead of page numbers?
options: New tweets shift offset pages, causing duplicates and gaps
quiz.why: Time-ordered IDs give a stable 'older than X' boundary.

quiz.q: A user deletes a tweet that is already in 3M cached timelines. Best approach?
options: LREM it from all 3M lists synchronously
Mark it deleted and filter during hydration
quiz.why: You hydrate every ID anyway, so filtering there is free and immediate.

quiz.q: Why return 201 to the poster before fan-out finishes?
options: Fan-out can take seconds and the poster shouldn't wait for it
quiz.why: Eventual consistency on followers' feeds is acceptable; the durable write already happened.
